title: Scaling Up, Speeding Up: Speculative Decoding for LLM Test-Time Scaling
one_liner: When reasoning takes multiple steps, simple pattern-matching can guess ahead safely, cutting compute cost in half.
lead: Large language models now spend reasoning time by running many inference passes — trying different answers, thinking through steps, or sampling alternatives. This sounds smart but wastes computation because the model keeps repeating the same phrases. The paper discovers that simple, dumb pattern-matching (looking for repeated sequences) can predict what comes next almost as well as the model can, letting you skip the expensive forward pass and just verify a guess.

paras: When you ask a language model (a system that predicts the next word) to reason or think through a problem, you run the whole model many times — once to generate each answer or reasoning step. This is expensive because the graphics card has to process every token (word or piece of a word) through every layer.

The naive approach: ask the model for the next token 100 times, wait for 100 full results. The model sees that it says the same phrase in every branch — 'let me work through this' appears identically in both answer attempts. Yet it re-computes from scratch each time, burning electricity on redundant arithmetic.

callout.html: During test-time scaling, language models generate highly repetitive reasoning traces, wasting computation on patterns the system will produce the same way each time.

steps.text: When the model generates token 47 given the prefix 'question is', store that link.
Next pass hits the same prefix; check the table before calling the expensive inference.
If the table says token 47, output it tentatively; if it does not, call the full model.
Feed the guessed token back; the model's next step confirms it was right or wrong.

steps.b: Build the table as you go
steps.text: Each new pass adds more prefix-to-token links, making future guesses more likely to hit.

paras: The paper measures three families of methods to guess the next token without a full model forward pass: models trained to predict next tokens (model-based), learnable routing weights (training-based), and simple dictionary lookups from past sequences (n-gram-based). The core move is the benchmark itself — a consistent test to compare them fairly.

hidden.name: fraction of tokens matching the history
paras: The paper's key discovery is that reasoning traces are not uniform; some parts repeat exactly. The hidden quantity is how often the model, given a prefix it has seen before, produces the exact same next token. If you see 'Question: what is 2+2' five times across different answer attempts, it almost always generates 'Answer:' next — that match rate is high.

The paper measures this by counting when a pattern-match lookup (n-gram method) succeeds — when the exact prefix reappears and the predicted token agrees with what the model later produces. High repetition density means simple lookup tables capture the model's behavior cheaply; low density means the model is reasoning differently each time, requiring expensive forward passes.

heat.caption: Dark cells: phrases repeated across reasoning attempts. Light cells: unique to one branch. Tables work best for dark regions.

reads.html: Reasoning and thinking do not start fresh each time — the model says the same thing in similar contexts, and we can memorize and reuse it.
Speculative decoding success depends on the overlap between reasoning trajectories. High n-gram match rates reveal the structural redundancy the paper exploits.

paras: When a language model reasons, it operates token-by-token, and each token is computed by running data through many layers of arithmetic on the graphics card. These layers multiply numbers and add them up — the core work the model does. This is expensive. But the model's predictions are deterministic — the same context always gives the same output (in greedy mode). So if you have seen a long prefix before, the next token is guaranteed to be identical.

Speculative decoding trades off computation: store every prefix and its successor, then check the table before running the model. For repeated reasoning (setup phrases, verification steps, common reasoning scaffolds), this table lookup is millions of times faster than a full inference pass because checking a hash table is pure memory access, while running the model means thousands of arithmetic operations on the graphics card. The model is only called when the table has no answer, which becomes increasingly rare as reasoning fills in the table. The mechanism works because reasoning is structured and repetitive by nature — you state the problem the same way each time, verify the same way, and scaffold the same way.

When you integrate n-gram methods with model-based guessing, you capture the redundancy where it exists (common phrases) and switch to expensive prediction only for reasoning that has never appeared before. This is why the paper finds that n-gram methods alone are effective, but combining them with trained predictors is even better: together they cover both repetitive and original reasoning.

stages.s: Prefix from reasoning so far, 'Question: what is 2+2? Answer:'
Check: have we seen this exact prefix in any earlier pass?
If yes, table lookup returns the next token instantly (table hit).
If no, call the full model (expensive forward pass, table miss).
Output: next token. Store this prefix-to-token pair for future passes.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose: 100 tokens generated, 80 table hits, 20 model passes.
Cost per table hit: 1 unit (instant). Cost per model pass: 1000 units (GPU arithmetic).
Speedup: 100,000 / 20,080 ≈ 5x. If reasoning were 95% repetitive: (95 * 1) + (5 * 1000) = 5,095 units, speedup ≈ 20x.

math.note: The speedup depends entirely on repetition density — how many tokens the model outputs identically given the same prefix.

items.html: If the model's reasoning is highly exploratory and new each time (low repetition density), tables stay sparse. Table hits become rare, and the speedup collapses to nearly zero.

items.b: Table becomes outdated when model changes.
items.html: If the model's outputs change after fine-tuning or prompting shifts, old table entries become stale — they say token 47 when the model now outputs token 23. Speculative decoding then produces wrong tokens.
Storing every prefix seen in a large-scale reasoning run can consume significant memory. Naive lookup tables scale poorly, requiring clever hash structures or caching policies.

Build tables for each reasoning type and scenario separately. Monitor repetition density; if low, skip speculative decoding. Verify predictions online; if the model later contradicts the table, discard that entry.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple experiment: (1) Use a small language model or a frozen pretrained model. (2) Generate reasoning traces for multiple test examples (e.g., step-by-step math or question-answering). (3) Collect all prefix-to-token pairs from the first pass. (4) On the second pass, intercept each generation request: before calling the model, check if the prefix is in the table. If yes, output the predicted token and skip the model. If no, call the model and store the new pair. (5) Measure time and output a match-rate histogram (how many prefixes repeated).
demo.closing: The demo must make impossible to miss: when reasoning is repetitive, table hits are frequent, inference is dramatically faster (because skipping the model's arithmetic layers saves orders of magnitude of compute), and the output is identical to what the model would produce.
